subtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER ON CROWN CORPORATIONS IN INTERNATIONAL TRADE

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER ON CROWN CORPORATIONS IN INTERNATIONAL TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are all aware that an increasingly competitive atmosphere in international trade has led in the post-war period to trading arrangements and business practices which are not always in keeping with the legal and ethical standards of Canada and other countries. In recent years, both the private and public sectors in several countries have been working toward an improved code of conduct governing the promotion of international trade. Accordingly, I wish to state today the policy of the government of Canada on the conduct which is expected of Canadian Crown corporations and, more particularly, on the commercial practices of these corporations.
To put the issue in perspective, we must recognize as a fact of life the constant tension between the twin goals of promot-
December 16, 1976

ing foreign trade and, at the same time, maintaining standards of conduct on the part of Canadians and their agents which can stand up to the closest public scrutiny. This is not a new problem, nor is it restricted, in its broader dimensions, to the field of international trade. Each of us is familiar, in our own lives, with the way in which our ethical judgments define acceptable and unacceptable methods of pursuing personal goals. In the process of making such judgments, both governments and individuals discern that some actions are clearly unacceptable because they are obviously in conflict either with the law of the land or with fundamental principles of behaviour which individuals or societies have adopted as their own. Other actions are just as clearly discerned to be perfectly consistent with both the law and ethical principles.
But there is a middle area, a grey area, where difficulties can, and do, arise. In this middle area fall those practices about which people who consider themselves to be of equal integrity can make differing judgments, practices whose ethical quality can be perceived differently in different societies, and even within the same society at different stages of its development. The existence of this grey area demands that those responsible for the conduct of others provide guidance. It demands, as well, that such guidance be re-examined periodically to keep it relevant to changing circumstances, maturing values, and newly developed practices. For an exporting country like Canada, whose economic health is largely determined by its success in selling its goods and services abroad, the way in which that trade is carried out is of major importance to the country as a whole. That is why the government of Canada is heavily involved, and properly so, in promoting our products and helping private Canadian companies to sell their goods and services to foreign customers. In the case of Crown corporations involved in the export trade, the level of government involvement in sales promotion and trade is even more pronounced.
To appreciate how vital these efforts are to the economy of the country, one need only note that 25 per cent of all jobs in Canada are related to our export trade, as is some 23 per cent of the income of Canadians and about 56 per cent of the goods produced in this country. Because international trade is a matter of economic life or death for Canada, the government and the people of this country are naturally concerned about any development which might jeopardize our trading activity or damage our external and trade relations. In the recent past, we have had reason for concern.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER ON CROWN CORPORATIONS IN INTERNATIONAL TRADE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. First among these concerns there have been, over the past few years, revelations about unacceptable business practices, including bribery,
Guidelines for Crown Corporations which involved corporations and governments in other parts of the world. These revelations have shocked the international community, disrupted governments and cast a disturbing shadow over the international trading environment. In response, the governments of Canada and other countries have taken remedial action. The international community, within the United Nations and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, is making a determined effort to establish a code of conduct suited to the problems which have come to our attention. Canada has supported, and will continue to support, such efforts.
The second reason for concern is that here at home questions have recently been raised about the business and accounting practices of certain Crown corporations involved in the export trade, such as Polysar and Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. In response, the government has referred these questions to the public accounts committee of the House. The government is giving the committee its full co-operation, in the confidence that we will receive sound and helpful advice at the conclusion of its deliberations. As a further response, the government has formalized the guidelines governing the commercial practices of federal Crown corporations. With a view to providing both protection and guidance, I will now state those guidelines: (1) in the process of doing business, officials of federal Crown corporations shall not, directly or indirectly, firstly, take any action in Canada that is not in accordance with the laws of Canada, or take any action outside Canada that violates the laws of the place where the transaction occurs, or that if taken in Canada would be in violation of the Criminal Code of Canada; secondly, render or accept any bribe or other improper benefit; or thirdly, apply improper influence.
Then (2) in retaining sales and procurement agents, Crown corporations shall adhere to the following principles: first, the matter of selection of those agents. Crown corporations must adopt an established selection process to ensure that the agent's qualifications for the work are clearly established and evaluated. Second, the process of contracting: (a) agency agreements shall be formally written and shall include specific undertakings by the agents to act in accordance with the laws of the place where the transaction occurs; (b) remuneration under the agreements shall be based on justifiable and sound business practice; (c) payments shall be strictly in accordance with the formal written agreement.
In terms of approval of those contracts: (a) the board of directors or other governing body of each corporation shall establish a procedure for approval of agency agreements; (b) the board of directors or other governing body may approve any exception from the administrative aspects of this policy where it is satisfied such exception is warranted. On the matter of disclosure: (a) corporations will disclose in their annual reports the names of their agents, as well as the aggregate of all remuneration paid to such agents; (b) any approved administrative exception from the policy and the reasons therefor shall be disclosed in the annual report of the corporation.

December 16, 1976
Guidelines for Crovm Corporations
Such is the government's policy and such are the guidelines governing the commercial practices of Crown corporations. I shall communicate them, in my capacity as President of the Treasury Board, to all departments and agencies listed in schedules A and B of the Financial Administration Act. The responsible ministers will likewise communicate them to all Crown corporations and agencies listed in schedules C and D of that act. These corporations will also be notified that the government will, if necessary, contemplate further action, including legislation, to ensure compliance with the policy I have just enunciated. Furthermore, the government will use its shareholder's prerogative, in other corporations where it has some degree of ownership or control, to ensure that they conform to the spirit of this policy.
The problems faced by Crown corporations are in many respects shared by departmental officials, such as diplomats and trade commissioners who assist in the promotion of Canadian exports. The principles that have governed in the past the activities of these public servants have been that, while these officials must do all they can to inform Canadian businessmen of all factors that could influence their sales prospects, they must, of course, limit their assistance to providing information of a general and factual nature, and must under no circumstances counsel or advise the businessman to engage in any corrupt or illegal practice.
I wish to inform the House that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has instructed the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) to ensure that procedures and practices in their departments continue to be consistent with the policy I have stated for Crown corporations. Needless to say, the government will welcome advice from the public accounts committee, other members of this House, the private sector and the general public on the ways in which guidelines for federal Crown corporations might be further improved and give even greater assurance of adherence to the rules I have just stated. Ministers responsible for the various aspects of our international trade have also been asked to review this matter and to recommend, as required, further improvement to the guidelines.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize that rigorous ethical standards and dedication to propriety-whether on the part of individuals, corporations, governments or nations- carry with them acceptance of certain practical limitations on action and performance. In other words, what I am really saying today is that, while we Canadians need and want to expand our foreign trade, we are not prepared to sell our goods and services on any terms or under any conditions. Principles, just as commodities, can be expensive. We Canadians must be fully aware of the price we must pay to live by our principles, to be the kind of people we want to be and to maintain the kind of society we want to have. We do not claim that the Canadian way of doing things and doing business makes us any better than other peoples or other countries. But it is the Canadian way-the way we have chosen for ourselves.

No central government agency recognizes the need to identify all corporations owned or controlled by the government of Canada.
Commercial enterprises in the private sector are subject to a greater degree of financial accountability than Crown corporations.
Financial management and control is not a priority within Crown corporations.
The annual deficits and net debt of the Government of Canada are substantially understated due to the manner of accounting for Crown corporations.
Parliament is presented with incomplete and fragmented financial plans and inadequate financial reports.
Financing practices would preclude evaluating management performance even if central agencies had the responsibility to do so.

First of all, in dealing with guideline number one, it would appear that this represents a complete shift from the position taken by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) in the House last week when he compared our business practices to the matter of the morality of adults in the bedrooms of the nation, and it was not our business to condemn the morals of anybody . Guidelines for Crown Corporations clearly the kind of shilly-shally approach this government has taken toward the conduct of Crown corporations.
Dealing with the question of agencies, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the guidelines outlined in respect of the use of agencies are pretty clear and fundamental. It might be well for the minister to add a guideline to ensure that these Crown corporations find out who are the agents, and if in fact they are employing real agents. Speaking of agents, I am sure I speak for many members of the House when I express concern about our not using facilities at our disposal, facilities such as the Canadian Commercial Corporation, embassies, or trade missions. Many of us feel that instead of employing on a wide scale agents for furthering our export endeavours, we should utilize Crown corporations such as the Canadians Commercial Corporation, trade missions and embassies.
I now come to the question of disclosure. Surely this matter is at the root of our problem. The question of Crown corporations' accountability to parliament has long been an outstanding one. Year after year Crown corporations present annual reports which are not referred to an appropriate parliamentary committee. I cite Air Canada as an example. The annual report of Air Canada was last submitted to the appropriate standing committee of this House in November, 1973. That is too long ago. Surely we should scrutinize the operations of that $1 billion enterprise which touches the lives of almost all Canadians in this country. But that corporation was not given the opportunity to appear before a parliamentary committee. We, as parliamentarians, are not given the opportunity regularly to question the operation of such Crown corporations. Surely we, the representatives of the shareholders of this Crown corporation, and others, are entitled to examine such operations regularly.
In my view, there ought to be provision for automatic reference to an appropriate standing committee. That, surely, is a minimum requirement. It should be up to the committee to decide if it wants to call members of the Crown corporation to appear, to give evidence or other testimony. Second, I suggest that this House should seriously consider establishing a permanent standing committee on Crown corporations, a committee with terms of reference broader than those applying to any other standing committee of the House of Commons. It would need such terms of reference in order to probe in depth and detail the conduct and operations of Crown corporations. Such a committee also must be given power to initiate studies on its own behalf.
I have suggested two or three steps which, if taken, would make Crown corporations more readily accountable to parlia-

ment and, thereby, to the people of Canada. I say with sadness that while this government has been in office, day by day the requirement with regard to accountability has been diminished. If Crown corporations are to be accountable to parliament and to respective committees, the process must begin with the restoration of parliamentary control over spending. The government must be held accountable to parliament, since that is at present where the difficulty lies. We must immediately begin reversing the present process, the process which has allowed the government to chip away the powers of parliament. That process has been escalated under the present regime. We must act immediately if we are to bring under control and impose a semblance of financial management on not only Crown corporations but on all departments and agencies of government.
Last, I say that this government must immediately implement all recommendations of the Auditor General because they are part and parcel of the question of accountability. Not until we restore the powers of parliament will we restore the confidence of Canadians in our institutions, management and control systems and Crown corporations.

We have run into the problem which we have with our existing Crown corporations, with AECL and with Polysar, as the Auditor General reported, because this government has lost control over the financial operations of the country.
The government, in statements made by the Prime Minister in reply to questions in the House, has said that they have informal rules already, that Crown corporations and depart-

December 16, 1976

merits have been aware of these regulations for some time. If they already have these guidelines, then how have we got into the mess in which we now find ourselves? Is the production of this paper by the minister, this nice enunciation in formal form, to use his phrase, going to prevent what seems clearly to have occurred in the past? Not at all. We should have no confidence in that, nor does the Auditor General, or we would not have had the report we have that the government has lost control of the financial operations of this country for which they are responsible.
I say, then, on behalf of the NDP, by all means let us have these guidelines-we are not going to quibble about them-it is a reasonable statement, but they will mean nothing but pious platitudes unless the government moves to correct and improve the enforcement procedures. What does this mean? It seems to me that they should accept the central recommendation in the Auditor General's report to bring in a comptroller general. One of his specific functions should be the mandate to enforce these guidelines. That would put some teeth in the guidelines; it might make them operative. As has been suggested by the minister who introduced the guidelines today, they have no teeth. Secondly, we suggest, as we did in a motion that was put before the House two weeks ago, that all these annual reports of Crown corporations be submitted automatically to one of the standing committees of the House.
The Conservative Party has spoken in favour of this idea as well. The opposition is making what seems to be a reasonable case here. Let us exercise our responsibility on this side of the House by having these reports come automatically to a standing committee of the House so that we can ex post facto look at the operations of the Crown corporations. But in expressing this, I must underscore the first point. We do not want to catch the damage only after it has been done. We want to set up a procedure in advance to stop improper behaviour. Therefore, the first point is the key one; that is, to appoint a comptroller general, a man or woman who would be responsible for enforcing these good guidelines which otherwise will be just pious platitudes.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people are now going through moments of reflections which, to my mind, are priceless. The statement of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) really impressed me because it contains observations that are extremely valuable and stands of which not only the heads of Crown companies should be made aware but also all Canadians, whether they be in the public or the private sectors.
That statement deserves to be read and reread and, later on, implemented. The first paragraph, Mr. Speaker, reads as follows, and I quote:
We are all aware that an increasingly competitive atmosphere in international trade has led in the post-war period to trading arrangements and business practices which are not always in keeping with the legal and ethical standards of Canada and other countries.
To my mind, what should first hold our attention in that paragraph is the fact that it has been noticed that since the
Guidelines for Crown Corporations war, Canada, like other countries, has become better known throughout the world, and that this is one of the positive results of the war of 1939-45.
After the war, which the Allies won, and which Germany lost, the defeated country outdid us. The Germans did not stop to complain about their defeat: they applied themselves to achieving results in their country, to rebuilding and reconquering international markets to the extent where today it lends money to the winning countries, including Canada. There is a lesson we should learn from the period that followed the Second World War. But we must not stop there. Our country benefitted from it, in that many countries discovered Canada and found out that they could obtain products made in Canada to meet their needs.
Since international trade is done through the private sector and Crown corporations, competition between both sectors is normal, and I think that it is even beneficial. Still, both must consider the quality of goods available and also fair dealings in transactions so that countries dealing with Canada through the private sector or Crown corporations will not feel-I almost had the intention of using a Canadian colloquialism-that they have been had . . . Well, that is honesty!

subsubtopic: CIDA-GRANT SYSTEM
speechtext: Does CIDA participate in a matching grant system or a similar type programme with the provinces where individual donations to foreign aid is matched by a provincial government and the provincial government donation matched by CIDA and, if so, with which provinces?

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CIDA-GRANT SYSTEM
speechtext: CIDA does participate in a program whereby matching contributions are made by some provincial governments to non-governmental organizations within their respective provinces for the purpose of carrying out mutually agreed upon projects in developing countries. CIDA will match the total funds put in by the NGO and the provincial government. This arrangement obtains in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. In Manitoba and Saskatchewan, the arrangement provides for the provincial government to give matching funds to NGO's for approved projects, provided that CIDA also agrees to contribute to the project. The formula is CIDA 50 per cent; private funds 25 per cent; provincial government 25 per cent. Alberta will match NGO's contributions for projects whether or not CIDA contributes. If any project falls within CIDA guidelines, a CIDA contribution may be made to the project, in which case the formula is the same as with Manitoba and Saskatchewan, i.e. CIDA 50 per cent; private funds 25 per cent; provincial government 25 per cent. In British Columbia, the provincial government has no maximum percentage of contribution to a project and therefore CIDA agrees to match provincial funds in each project only up to the amount of the NGO's contribution.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my party, I intend to take the time of the House now to explain once again why we are basically opposed to this bill proceeding further at the present time. What is the essence of the so-called restraint bill we are considering? What it amounts to is a demonstration by the government, along with its controls package, that it has decided to fight inflation on the back of the ordinary people of Canada. Where are the cutbacks in this restraint bill? First, in the area of family allowances, millions of dollars will be cut from the resources of the average family during the last 12 months as a result of this legislation. As the minister knows, and as he knew when he introduced the bill, the majority of those families are, by definition, average income or low income families. So that is the group most affected. The central aspect of the bill is that it cuts out the escalation which would automatically have been forthcoming in connection with family allowances and which would have enabled ordinary families better to cope with inflation in the last 12 months.
What else was cut? We closed down the Company of Young Canadians, a group which was doing some exceptional work in isolated or distant parts of the country-distant, that is, in the main from urban centres.
December 16, 1976

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext: In urban centres, too.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
I said, "in the main outside the urban centres". But I agree that good work has been done in the cities too. The bill also removed the LIP program: I note it is now coming back. The manpower training program was modified in a significant way. I could list other aspects of the restraints imposed by the bill, but I have done enough to make my central point: the cutbacks were precisely in areas which affected those who needed assistance, rather than a restraint program imposed upon them by the federal government. The other side of the coin concerns that part of the federal government's operations which are not affected. There was no curtailment of the excessive use of office space so well documented in the recent report of the Auditor General. There was no commitment to cut back on appointments of civil servants earning $20,000 and more which have mushroomed so significantly in the past half-dozen years in Ottawa. In other words, no attention was paid to introducing restrictions in areas of government outlay where such programs would have been justified, or where such restraints would have affected upper income groups more markedly than those in lower income groups.
Therefore, in stressing our opposition to this bill we connect it with the generally inequitable nature of the government's anti-inflation program as a whole. I would remind Your Honour that connected with this legislation were other measures; for example, a measure cutting back medical research, work which has a profound impact upon the lives of Canadians, if not immediately then in the years or decades ahead. From the government's point of view, cutting down research is, of course, an easy thing to do politically because most people do not consider themselves directly affected. It is a cheap kind of cutback, the sort which is done with safety from a political point of view, but it does harm in the long run, particularly to a country which already has a bad reputation as an industrial society in terms of percentage of gross national product going into medical or scientific research.
Related to this package was the surtax bill introduced last year. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) told us almost a year ago, if I remember correctly, that he was imposing a surtax on the rich to make sure they assumed their share of the burden of the war against inflation. Well, it was not much of a burden as a component of the war fought by other Canadians. But even so, this party believes it to be a disgraceful act on the part of the government to have declared its intention, now, to abolish that surtax for the coming fiscal year. The minister and his friends are not abolishing other aspects of the restraint program. The most significant anti-inflation device put in place by the government is, of course, the wage control program, and this is to remain indefinitely. But the small tax which was imposed on upper income Canadians, presumably for the duration of the restraint program, comes to an end this fiscal year. We find this totally inexcusable.
I also believe it is proper at this time, the government having maintained a control program which is effective in holding down increases in the wages and salaries of ordinary Canadi-
Restraint of Government Expenditures
ans, to say something about our own salaries as members of parliament. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) has just got up to leave, I notice. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has already asked the minister whether anything is to be done about the salaries of members of parliament, in general, for the coming year. The answer was no, they would be permitted the normal increase. However, the point I want to make is that there are a lot of members in this House. I am not referring to ordinary members; I am referring to party leaders, to parliamentary secretaries, to members of the cabinet, to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-they would get increases in excess of the $2,400 ceiling.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I now have the support of all members of the House, having made that comment.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext: You want it for yourself, though.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
The point I want to make is that if there is a $2,400 ceiling for ordinary workers, then contrary to what a Liberal member opposite says, the members of my party believe that the $2,400 ceiling should hold for the members of the House of Commons as well. The Minister of Finance is talking to another cabinet colleague, but if I may have his attention for a moment I appeal to him to exercise whatever influence he might have in the cabinet to ensure that his cabinet colleagues and parliamentary secretaries, who are sitting in the House today, as well as the party leaders, get no increase in excess of the $2,400. If it is fair outside the House, then, as I have said, it is fair inside the House.
To underscore our opposition to the restraints bill as strongly as I can, if the Prime Minister will not listen to suggestions made by the New Democratic Party, then I appeal to Liberals to yield for once to their normal impulse to follow everything that goes on in the United States. Normally we do not like to suggest this, but there is one thing now going on as a matter of political orientation with which we agree, and that is that the President elect of the United States, Mr. Carter, has recognized that the central economic problem in North America today is not inflation; that the central problem we have to face in our society is not increases in prices but it is that we have almost one million people out of work.
The President elect of the United States has said he is going to set unemployment targets in his country. Two months ago the New Democratic Party proposed that this government set targets for unemployment-not pie in the sky-which would bring unemployment down 2 per cent over the next two years and another 2 per cent over the following two years, which would mean that over a four-year period we would have a commitment to full employment. The President elect of the United States has recognized that this is the problem and he is taking it on.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
And he is right.

speechtext: A Liberal says that he is right. I hope he can influence his cabinet friends. The President elect has said that there will be a tax cut in the United States; he has said that he will allocate special funds to federal programs from one end of the United States to the other in order to create jobs. That is what this government should be doing, Mr. Speaker. The people of Canada want jobs-they are tired of hand-outs-and that is what this party stands for. The present level of unemployment in Canada is costing us $6 billion a year in lost production of goods and services. We are losing almost $1 billion in tax revenue which men and women would be paying into the treasury to provide services for the people of Canada. We are also losing about $2 billion which is spent on welfare payments and on unemployment insurance, directly attributable to the unemployment level. The cost of unemployment is profound. Every man and woman in this country who wants to work ought to be able to work. There is no excuse in an advanced industrial society which has any guts or any serious commitment to economic planning for the present level of unemployment.

A Liberal says he has heard enough. It is very difficult for the Liberal mind, Mr. Speaker, to try to absorb anything for more than 30 seconds. With anything of substance it takes only 15 seconds before their attention wanes. I think it is instructive to note that the backbenchers of the Liberal party agree that we need to do something about unemployment, but the closer they get to the front benches, to become parliamentary secretaries or cabinet members, they begin to say that we need not be concerned. I know which group over there is in touch with the people of Canada, and they are not those who sit in the front row, Mr. Speaker.
We in the New Democratic Party say that the time for restraint, as a preoccupation of government, adopting the attitude that we have cut back right across the line, is over. What we need now is some imagination and leadership which will produce jobs in this country. In concluding my observations on this absurd bill, I want to remind the House that we have been here for two months. Do hon. members on the other side know how many bills the House of Commons has passed in two months? Two, Mr. Speaker. One bill had to do with the harbour in Halifax, a minor bill but dealing with a serious
situation which, I recall, had the support of all members of the House. One other bill has been passed. We are going to be away, within three or five days, for a month. We have a government which is still preoccupied with restraint and has had nothing but housekeeping measures to bring before parliament this session. It has shown the dramatic leadership that is required to achieve passage of two bills in two months. In the meantime-

speechtext: It is your party that wants another holiday.

speechtext:
If the noisy jackals on the other side would listen, they might learn something. While the government has done nothing, almost one million Canadians have been unemployed. If you count the number of people indirectly affected, be they wives or in some cases husbands and children, a minimum of 2.5 million Canadians this Christmas will be in not so merry a condition. These people can be found in every town, village and province as well as the territories of this country. While President elect Carter has recognized the need for leadership, the cabinet we have in Ottawa sits and wallows in its own, shall I say, contentment, its own colossal indifference. We have an indifferent government on the other side, and I have not the slightest doubt about the political impact of this indifference, not only over the Christmas season but in the months beyond. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
